1F (Linear Algebra)

1F OurBigBook.com
Use completing the square rather than computing the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix. Successively removing the mixed terms gives
q=2(x+2y−23​z)2−7y2+8yz−25​z2=2(x+2y−23​z)2−7(y−74​z)2−143​z2.
(1)
Thus one suitable invertible linear change of coordinates is
X=x+2y−23​z,Y=y−74​z,Z=z;q=2X2−7Y2−143​Z2.​
(2)
The coordinate matrix is upper triangular with determinant one, so the change is an invertible linear map. Its inverse is z=Z, y=Y+4Z/7, x=X−2Y+5Z/14. Hence the diagonal coefficients can be taken as 2,−7,−3/14. This is a matrix congruence of a quadratic form; an orthogonal transformation was not required.

2E (Groups, Rings and Modules)

Words: 173 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 173
2E OurBigBook.com
The fraction field of an integral domain R is a field F containing an identified copy of R in which every element has the form a/b with a,b∈R and b=0. Equality means a/b=c/d exactly when ad=bc; the operations are the usual addition and multiplication of fractions. We use unital ring homomorphisms.
Since φ is injective, φ(b)=0 whenever b=0. Define
Φ(a/b)=φ(a)φ(b)−1.​
(3)
If ad=bc, applying the ring homomorphism and dividing by φ(b)φ(d) proves the value is independent of the representative. The fraction addition and multiplication rules show that Φ preserves both operations and one, and Φ(a/1)=φ(a). If Φ(a/b)=0, then φ(a)=0, so a=0 because φ is an injective function; therefore its kernel is zero and Φ is injective. It is also the unique extension, because any ring homomorphism extending φ must send b−1 to φ(b)−1.
For a counterexample, take R=Z, F=Q, and reduction modulo two ψ:Z→Z/2Z. An extension would give 1=Ψ(2)Ψ(1/2)=0, a contradiction. Nonzero denominators must become invertible in the target; an arbitrary ring homomorphism need not have that property.

Differentiability here is understood in the sense of the Fréchet derivative: there is a linear map L:Rn→Rm such that
f(x+h)=f(x)+Lh+r(h),∥h∥∥r(h)∥​⟶0(h→0).​
(4)
The map L=Df(x) is the Fréchet derivative. In finite dimensions a linear map is bounded, so ∥Lh∥≤C∥h∥ for some C. The defining estimate therefore implies
∥f(x+h)−f(x)∥≤C∥h∥+o(∥h∥)⟶0.
(5)
This is precisely continuity at x: differentiability implies continuity.

4E (Metric and Topological Spaces)

Words: 244 Articles: 4
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 124 Articles: 1
4E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 124
a OurBigBook.com
Let K be a compact set of a Hausdorff space X. For any x∈/K and each y∈K, the Hausdorff property gives disjoint open sets Uy​∋y and Vy​∋x. The sets Uy​ cover K; compactness supplies a finite subcover Uy1​​,…,Uyr​​. The open set V=⋂i​Vyi​​ contains x and misses every Uyi​​, hence misses K. Thus X∖K is open, and every compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed. The empty-set case is immediate.
Since R with its usual topology is Hausdorff, its compact sets are closed. The open cover {(−n,n):n≥1} of R has a finite subcover of any compact set K. Taking the largest index in that subcover gives K⊂(−N,N), so K is a bounded set. This proves the required direction of the Heine-Borel theorem without assuming its converse.

Take X to be the set Q, equipped with the discrete metric
d(p,q)={0,1,​p=q,p=q.​f(p)=p∈Q.​
(11)
Every Cauchy sequence is eventually constant: its terms must eventually have mutual distance in this metric less than 1/2. Consequently X is a complete metric space. Its topology is the discrete topology, since every singleton is a ball of radius 1/2 and every subset is a union of such balls.
For the codomain use the usual subspace topology on Q. The inverse image of any open set there is a subset of the discrete X, hence is open. Therefore f is continuous and plainly surjective. A continuous image of a complete metric space need not be complete. The two occurrences of Q have different domain and codomain metrics.

5A OurBigBook.com
For the method of characteristics, parameterize by x; the characteristic curves satisfy
dxdy​=−2x,dxdu​=cosx.
(12)
Thus x2+y=C and u−sinx is constant on each characteristic curve. The general form in the quadrant is u=sinx+F(x2+y). The boundary condition gives F(s2)=coss−sins for every s≥0.
The characteristic curve through (x,y) meets the boundary at (s,0) with s=x2+y​≥x. Integrating backwards from that boundary value yields
u(x,y)=sinx+cosx2+y​−sinx2+y​.​
(13)
Indeed ∂x​−2x∂y​ annihilates x2+y and sends sinx to cosx, while on y=0 the expression reduces to cosx. Every characteristic in the quadrant meets the prescribed boundary, so its value is determined. The displayed solution is smooth away from the origin. At the origin the boundary is characteristic and the solution is continuous but has a singular inward y derivative; the differential equation is interpreted in the interior, with the boundary data attained continuously.

In SI units the Ampère-Maxwell equation is ∇×B=μ0​J+μ0​ε0​∂t​E. Since E=0, the displacement-current term vanishes and ∇×B=μ0​J. Apply Stokes theorem to an oriented surface S with positively oriented boundary C:
∮C​B⋅dℓ=∫S​(∇×B)⋅ndS=μ0​∫S​J⋅ndS.
(14)
Hence the integral form of Ampère's law is
∮C​B⋅dℓ=μ0​Ienclosed​.​
(15)
Here μ0​ is vacuum magnetic permeability, J is current density, and positive enclosed electric current is defined by the orientation of S.

For the field generated by the infinitely long, axially symmetric shell currents, axisymmetry and the right-hand rule give B=Bϕ​(r)eϕ​. A circular loop has ∮B⋅dℓ=2πrBϕ​(r). Its enclosed electric current is zero inside the inner shell, I between the shells and 2I outside both. Ampère's law therefore gives
B(r)=⎩⎨⎧​0,2πrμ0​I​eϕ​,πrμ0​I​eϕ​,​r<a,a<r<b,r>b.​​
(16)
The positive eϕ​ direction is counterclockwise viewed from positive z. The ideal current sheets make the tangential magnetic field discontinuous at each shell; these formulas specify the three open regions, with no additional imposed background field.

B(r)=⎩⎨⎧​0,2πrμ0​I​eϕ​,0,​r<a,a<r<b,r>b.​​
(17)
Opposite currents confine the generated magnetic field to the annulus, as in an ideal infinitely long coaxial cable. The two shell current sheets account for the field jumps.

For this steady unidirectional flow, the convective acceleration (u⋅∇)u vanishes because u depends only on y. The axial Navier-Stokes equation reduces to 0=−px​+μu′′, with px​=−G. The no-slip boundary conditions therefore give
μu′′(y)=−G,u(0)=0,u(h)=U.​
(18)
This is a superposition of Couette flow and pressure-driven Poiseuille flow.

Integrate the axial ordinary differential equation twice: u=−Gy2/(2μ)+C1​y+C2​. The no-slip boundary condition at zero gives C2​=0, and the one at h gives C1​=U/h+Gh/(2μ). Hence
u(y)=hU​y+2μG​y(h−y).​
(19)
The first term is Couette flow; the second is Poiseuille flow driven in positive x when G>0. Their addition is valid because the reduced Stokes equation is linear.

u′(0)=hU​+2μGh​,U=−2μGh2​.​

q=∫0h​u(y)dy=−6μGh3​.​

For G>0, the plate must move against the pressure-driven direction, and the resulting signed volume flux is negative. Zero bottom-wall shear does not mean zero flow.

8H (Statistics)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 138
8H OurBigBook.com
Under the null hypothesis the three outcome probabilities are the same in the two independent samples. The pooled row totals are 50,20,30, and both column totals are 50, out of a total of 100. Thus the expected counts in each column are 25,10,15. These exceed the usual small-count threshold for the asymptotic Pearson chi-squared test of homogeneity.
The Pearson chi-squared statistic for contingency tables is
X2=2(25(28−25)2​+10(4−10)2​+15(18−15)2​)=9.12​.
(22)
Under the null, its asymptotic chi-squared distribution has (3−1)(2−1)=2 degrees of freedom. Equivalently, the two independent three-category samples have four probability parameters unrestricted and two under the common-probability null. The 1% upper-tail critical value is 9.21.
Since 9.12<9.21, do not reject the equal-effect hypothesis at the 1% level. For two degrees of freedom, the approximate p-value is e−9.12/2≃0.01046, just above 0.01. This is a decision at the specified significance level, not evidence that the two outcome distributions have been proved identical.

Introduce nonnegative slack variables s1​,s2​,s3​ and start the simplex algorithm at x=y=z=0, with slacks 9,8,2. The objective's largest positive entering coefficient belongs to y. Its ratio test is 9/3=3, 8/2=4, 2/1=2, so s3​ leaves and y enters.
Solve that pivot row for y and substitute into the other rows and the objective v:
ys1​s2​v​=2−2x−3z−s3​,=3−2x−z+3s3​,=4−x+2z+2s3​,=10−7x−15z−5s3​.​
(23)
This is a feasible simplex dictionary at nonbasic variables x=z=s3​=0. All their objective coefficients are negative, so no feasible increase can improve the objective. Thus
(x,y,z)=(0,2,0),vmax​=10.​
(24)
The negative reduced coefficients also prove uniqueness of this optimum.
The dual linear program, with nonnegative variables u1​,u2​,u3​, is
minimize 9u1​+8u2​+2u3​,8u1​+5u2​+2u3​≥3,3u1​+2u2​+u3​≥5,10u1​+4u2​+3u3​≥0.​
(25)
The feasible choice (u1​,u2​,u3​)=(0,0,5)​ has objective 10. Weak duality proves that it and the primal point are optimal. Complementary slackness also forces u1​=u2​=0 because the first two primal slacks are positive, and then the positive y forces u3​=5.

Group the matrix entries by columns. Each column of BA is B times the corresponding column of A. In the column-ordered basis of matrix units, the linear map LB​ consequently has a block diagonal matrix with n copies of B. The determinant of a block diagonal matrix is the product of its block determinants, giving
detLB​=(detB)n.​
(26)

detMB​=(detB)n(detB)n=∣detB∣2n.​

If A is a Hermitian matrix, then (BAB∗)∗=BAB∗, so MB​ preserves W. Addition and multiplication by real scalars commute with this operation, making TB​ a real linear map.
A real basis of W consists of Eii​ and, for i<j, Eij​+Eji​ and i(Eij​−Eji​). It has n2 elements and is also a complex basis of all matrices. Indeed every matrix is uniquely H+iK with H,K Hermitian matrices, by taking
H=2A+A∗​,K=2iA−A∗​.
(28)
Real linear independence of the displayed basis therefore implies complex linear independence. Since its images under MB​ are Hermitian matrices, the matrix of MB​ in this complex basis has exactly the same real entries as the matrix of TB​ in the real basis. Their determinants are equal. There is no further squaring when passing to this real subspace:
detTB​=∣detB∣2n.​
(29)
This is the determinant of Hermitian congruence, including the case of singular B.

a OurBigBook.com
Write ∣G∣=prm with p prime and p∤m. The Sylow theorems assert that a subgroup of order pr exists; every p-group subgroup is contained in a conjugate of a Sylow subgroup; all Sylow subgroups are conjugate; and their number np​ satisfies np​≡1(modp) and np​∣m.
For the containment and conjugacy assertions, fix a Sylow subgroup P and let any p-group subgroup Q act by left multiplication on the m left cosets G/P. By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, every orbit has size a power of p. Since p∤m, at least one orbit has size one. If gP is such a fixed point, then qgP=gP for all q∈Q, equivalently g−1Qg⊆P. Thus Q⊆gPg−1. If Q too has order pr, this inclusion is equality, proving conjugacy. This is Sylow containment from a coset fixed point.

b

Words: 119 Articles: 1
11E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 119
b OurBigBook.com
Since 351=33⋅13, the number of Sylow subgroups for p=13 divides 27 and is 1 modulo 13, hence is 1 or 27. In the first case the unique subgroup is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup.
In the second case the 27 subgroups of order 13 have pairwise trivial intersection: two such subgroups sharing a nonidentity element would both be generated by it. They account for 27⋅12=324 nonidentity elements of order 13. Exactly 27 elements, including the identity, remain. Every Sylow subgroup for p=3 has order 27, and all its elements lie among these remaining elements, by Lagrange's theorem. It must therefore be precisely that set. The Sylow subgroup for p=3 is unique and hence normal. In either case G is not a simple group.

∣GL2​(F31​)∣=(312−1)(312−31)=27325231.
(30)
Since 53=125≡1(mod31) and 5=1, the residue 5 has order three. The nine diagonal matrices diag(5i,5j), with 0≤i,j<3, form a subgroup isomorphic to C3​×C3​. It is an abelian group and a Sylow subgroup for p=3. Every other Sylow subgroup for p=3 is conjugate to it by the Sylow theorems, hence is also Abelian.

A norm on a real or complex vector space V is a function ∥⋅∥:V→[0,∞) with ∥v∥=0 exactly when v=0, ∥λv∥=∣λ∣∥v∥, and the triangle inequality ∥v+w∥≤∥v∥+∥w∥. These are positivity, absolute homogeneity and the triangle inequality.

For a linear map A:Rm→Rn, define the operator norm by
∥A∥=x=0sup​∥x∥∥Ax∥​=∥x∥=1sup​∥Ax∥.​
(31)
It is finite. To see this without assuming continuity of A, write x=∑xj​ej​: the triangle inequality bounds ∥Ax∥ by ∑∣xj​∣∥Aej​∥. Every norm in finite dimensions is equivalent to the Euclidean norm. One proof first uses this same coordinate bound to establish continuity of the norm on the Euclidean unit sphere; compactness then gives a strictly positive minimum there. Thus the coordinate bound above is at most a fixed multiple of ∥x∥.
Absolute homogeneity and the triangle inequality for this operator norm follow from those for ∥Ax∥ and taking suprema. If ∥A∥=0, then Ax=0 for every x, hence A=0, and the converse is immediate. For any B:Rℓ→Rm, the defining bound ∥Ax∥≤∥A∥∥x∥ gives
∥ABx∥≤∥A∥∥Bx∥≤∥A∥∥B∥∥x∥,∥AB∥≤∥A∥∥B∥.​

This is submultiplicativity of the operator norm.

Put r=∥X∥<1. By submultiplicativity of the operator norm, ∥Xk∥≤rk, so the Neumann series converges absolutely in the complete finite-dimensional matrix space. Its partial sums satisfy
(I−X)∑k=0N​Xk=(∑k=0N​Xk)(I−X)=I−XN+1.
(34)
Taking limits gives the inverse and a quantitative remainder bound:
f(X)=k=0∑∞​Xk,​f(X)−k=0∑N​Xk​≤1−rrN+1​.​
(35)
To establish two actual Fréchet derivatives, use the resolvent identity
f(X+H)−f(X)=f(X+H)Hf(X).
(36)
For fixed X∈U and sufficiently small H, factor I−X−H=(I−X)(I−f(X)H) and apply the Neumann series to the second factor. This proves that X+H∈U, that f(X+H) is locally bounded, and that f(X+H)−f(X)=O(∥H∥). Subtracting f(X)Hf(X) in the identity leaves O(∥H∥2). Thus Df(X)[H]=f(X)Hf(X) is the Fréchet derivative.
Near zero, f(X)=I+X+O(∥X∥2), uniformly in the operator norm. Hence, as a linear operator in H,
Df(X)[H]=H+XH+HX+O(∥X∥2∥H∥).
(37)
This proves differentiability of Df at zero, giving
Df(0)[H]=H,D2f(0)[H,K]=HK+KH.​
(38)
The order of multiplication matters: the second Fréchet derivative is the symmetric bilinear map HK+KH, not 2HK.

At an interior point w of the geodesic segment from z1​ to z2​, the two angles made with the segment toward w′ add to π. At least one is at least π/2. In the corresponding hyperbolic triangle, part (a) says that its opposite side w′zi​ is at least the adjacent side w′w. Therefore
d(w′,w)≤max{d(w′,z1​),d(w′,z2​)}.​
(45)
If w is an endpoint the assertion is immediate. The same inequality also holds when w′ lies on the complete geodesic through z1​,z2​: parameterize that geodesic by arclength and use the elementary inequality ∣t−s∣≤max(∣t−a∣,∣t−b∣) for a≤s≤b. This extension will allow repeated use of the result in part (c).

Solution

Consider the filled hyperbolic triangle with vertices A,B,C. Every point P is on some geodesic segment Aw with w∈BC: for instance, in the Beltrami-Klein model these are the ordinary straight segments filling a convex triangle. For any other point Q of the triangle, apply part (b) first on Aw and then on BC:
d(Q,P)≤max{d(Q,A),d(Q,w)}≤max{d(Q,A),d(Q,B),d(Q,C)}.
(46)
Applying the same argument to Q, with each vertex held fixed, bounds every term on the right by the maximum of the three side lengths. The endpoints of a longest side attain that bound. Thus the diameter is exactly the longest side length:
diam(ABC)=max{d(A,B),d(B,C),d(C,A)}.​
(47)

With unit constant bending coefficients and unit length, the quadratic elastic energy is
E=21​∫01​(y′′2+z′′2−F(y′2+z′2))dx.
(51)
To find the first loss of positivity, put v=y′. The clamped conditions give v(0)=v(1)=0 and ∫01​vdx=0. Extend v periodically with period one. The sharp periodic Wirtinger inequality gives ∫01​v′2dx≥4π2∫01​v2dx. For completeness, expand the mean-zero periodic v in its Fourier series ∑n≥1​(an​cos2πnx+bn​sin2πnx). Parseval identity gives
∫01​v2dx=21​∑n≥1​(an2​+bn2​),∫01​v′2dx=21​∑n≥1​(2πn)2(an2​+bn2​),

Fc​=4π2,y=α(1−cos2πx),z=β(1−cos2πx).​
(54)
At this load every such pair has zero quadratic elastic energy and solves the Euler-Lagrange equations. For F>Fc​ these modes give negative energy, signaling instability of the straight configuration. The quadratic small-slope model does not select a finite post-buckling amplitude; nonlinear terms would be needed for that. This is Euler buckling of an elastic filament.

The Neumann boundary conditions select the spatial eigenfunctions cosnx, n=0,1,…, of the separated wave equation. Indeed separation gives X′′+λX=0 with X′(0)=X′(π)=0. Integration by parts gives λ∫X2=∫X′2≥0. The zero value yields the constant mode; for positive λ, the first boundary condition removes the sine term and the second requires λ​=n∈N. For n>0, the temporal factor is cosnct: the sine factor vanishes because the initial velocity is zero. The zero mode has constant displacement, with no term linear in time for the same reason.
The constant Fourier cosine series coefficient is the mean π−1∫0π​bxdx=bπ/2. The remaining coefficients are
an​=π2b​∫0π​xcosnxdx=πn22b​((−1)n−1).
(55)
Only odd modes survive. Thus the displacement is
y(x,t)=2bπ​−π4b​k=0∑∞​(2k+1)2cos((2k+1)x)cos((2k+1)ct)​.​
(56)
The series for displacement converges absolutely and uniformly. The initial velocity is zero in the finite-energy sense, and the initial displacement is bx. There is an endpoint compatibility qualification: when b=0, the initial slope does not satisfy the Neumann boundary conditions at t=0. The answer is therefore a finite-energy weak solution, piecewise classical between the propagating corners, rather than a globally twice continuously differentiable solution up to the initial endpoints. The mode expansion implements reflection at those endpoints.

The method of images for the Neumann boundary conditions extends bx evenly through zero and then with period 2π. Define the triangular wave
P(s)=b∣s−2kπ∣for (2k−1)π≤s≤(2k+1)π, k∈Z.​
(57)
The formulas agree at their endpoints. It is even, 2π-periodic, and agrees with bx on [0,π]. Its Fourier cosine series has the coefficients in part (a). The cosine product identity then gives the D'Alembert formula
y(x,t)=21​(P(x+ct)+P(x−ct)).​
(58)
It is the average of two oppositely traveling reflected waves. For b>0, the sketch rises from zero at even multiples of π to bπ at odd multiples; for b<0 it is reflected vertically, and for b=0 it is zero.

20H (Markov Chains)

Words: 476 Articles: 9
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 223 Articles: 1
20H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 223
a OurBigBook.com
Let C be an open communicating class, and fix i∈C. There is a path of positive probability from i to a state outside C. Choose a shortest such path, so it does not revisit i before exiting. No state reached outside C can have a path back to C: combined with the exit path and communication within C, such a path would put it in the same communicating class. Thus with positive probability the chain never returns to i. Its return probability is less than one, making i a transient state. This proves transience throughout C.
Conversely, suppose a finite communicating class were both closed and transient. Starting inside it, a path stays there forever. Since it has finitely many states, at least one state must be visited infinitely often. But a transient state is visited only finitely often almost surely, and the union of finitely many exceptional null events still has probability zero. This is a contradiction. Every finite transient communicating class is therefore open.
For the infinite counterexample, take the biased random walk on Z with independent increments +1 of probability 3/4 and −1 of probability 1/4. All states communicate, so Z is one infinite closed communicating class. The strong law of large numbers gives Xn​/n→1/2 almost surely. Consequently every fixed state is visited only finitely often, and the class is transient. Finiteness is exactly what fails in the preceding argument.

The only closed communicating class is {b,d}; the class {a,c} is open and transient. Its one-step probability of staying inside is at most 2/3, so if τ is the entrance time into {b,d}, then P(τ>n)≤(2/3)n for an initial state in {a,c}. Hence entrance occurs almost surely in finite time.
On {b,d} it is an irreducible aperiodic Markov chain, because both states have positive self-loop probabilities. The finite irreducible aperiodic countable-state Markov chain convergence theorem says that its transition probabilities converge to its unique stationary distribution. The balance equation πb​(3/4)=πd​(2/3) with πb​+πd​=1 gives πb​=8/17 and πd​=9/17.
This limit also holds from a,c: condition on the finite entrance time and entrance state. For τ≤M, convergence in the closed class applies to a finite sum; the remaining probability is bounded by P(τ>M), which tends to zero as M→∞. Thus in the order a,b,c,d,
n→∞lim​Pn=​0000​8/178/178/178/17​0000​9/179/179/179/17​​.​
